title: Free time: relaxation and leisure
subtitle: rewarding, a culture vulture, hooked on
summary: Describe hobbies and free-time activities with precise adjectives, and talk about the kind of person you are in your leisure time using colourful informal expressions.

lesson.heading: Adjectives describing free-time activities
rows: gives you a lot of positive experiences
makes you healthy in body and/or mind
reduces stress, gives a peaceful feeling
takes a long time to do
being president of a club, sitting on a committee

lesson.heading: Using the adjectives
lesson.text: These adjectives sit in front of words like *activity*, *pursuit*, *experience* and *hobby*, or after *be*. Notice that **rewarding** is about how you feel, while **lucrative** is only about money - they are not the same thing.

examples.text: I enjoyed being secretary of the sports club but it was very **time-consuming**. I had to give up two evenings a week to do it.
The conservation work I do is very **rewarding**. I feel I'm doing something good and useful.
Photography has been a **lucrative** pursuit for her. She often sells her pictures to magazines.
Painting is such a **therapeutic** activity. It makes me feel good, and teaches me patience.

lesson.heading: Informal names for types of person
rows: a big fan of anything cultural - theatre, galleries, concerts
a physically very inactive person who watches a lot of TV
someone who does an activity as a hobby, not as a job
someone who never keeps doing one activity for long

lesson.heading: Talking about these people
lesson.text: All of these expressions are informal and slightly humorous. You often soften them with *a bit of a* or strengthen them with *a real*.

examples.text: Rob's **a real culture vulture**; he goes to the theatre regularly and to every art gallery he can find.
I'm **a bit of a couch potato**; I spend hours every day just watching TV.
Fatima's **a bit of a dabbler**; she takes up a hobby for a couple of weeks, then gets bored and starts something different.
Lucy loves playing tennis but only as an **amateur** - she'd never want to be a professional.
Mark is a **keen participant** in all the community activities in his town.

lesson.heading: Getting into things - and going off them
lesson.text: A set of everyday verb phrases describes how your enthusiasm for an activity grows or fades. They are all informal and extremely common in conversation.

examples.text: Joe is **heavily into** downhill skiing these days.
examples.note: be into something = be very involved in it

examples.text: He's totally **hooked on** motor racing these days.
examples.note: be hooked on = be addicted to

examples.text: I **went off** football and I **took up** golf instead.
examples.note: go off = stop liking, lose interest in; take up = start a new hobby

examples.text: She **locks herself away** for hours in her room and listens to music.
examples.note: lock yourself away = isolate yourself from the world

lesson.heading: Busy diaries and boring jobs
lesson.text: Two more useful areas: asking what someone does with their free time, and the unglamorous jobs that fill it.

examples.text: What do you **get up to** at weekends, Mariana?
Do you have a **hectic social life**? I have a pretty **full diary**.
examples.note: both mean you have a lot of activities

examples.text: Matt does a lot of **chores** at the weekend - things like shopping and **mowing the lawn**.
examples.note: chores = boring tasks that have to be done; a lawn is an area of cut grass

lesson.text: Words like *shopaholic*, *workaholic* and *chocaholic* are light-hearted inventions - unlike *alcoholic*, which names a serious, medically recognised condition.

exercises.prompt: Solve the riddles. Match each description with the person it describes.

pairs.left: I am a vegetable that sits where humans sit.
I enjoy shopping a bit too much.
I am a bird that eats the flesh of art.
I do some of this and some of that, but never all of either.
I play every week, but nobody ever pays me.

exercises.prompt: I find writing poetry very ___. It helps me to get a truer understanding of myself and gives me a good feeling inside.
exercises.explanation: Therapeutic activities make you healthy in body and/or mind.

exercises.prompt: I enjoy selling the pictures I paint, but it's not very ___. I only made £300 last year.
exercises.explanation: Lucrative means it makes a lot of money - which £300 a year clearly does not.

exercises.prompt: I've had a ___ partnership with Jane for several years: she plays the piano and I play the violin. It's been very good for both of us.
exercises.explanation: A fruitful collaboration is one that produces good results for everyone involved.

exercises.prompt: Doing unpaid work at the hospital has been a ___ experience for me.
exercises.explanation: The work is unpaid, so it cannot be lucrative; rewarding means it gives you a lot of positive experiences.

exercises.prompt: I would like to be on the club committee, but I've heard it's very ___, and I don't have a lot of free time.
exercises.explanation: Time-consuming activities eat up large amounts of your time.

exercises.prompt: Does each expression describe an activity or a person?

exercises.statement: An amateur footballer gets paid for playing a match.
exercises.explanation: No - an amateur plays as a hobby, not as a job. A professional gets paid.

exercises.statement: If you say that someone dabbles in photography, you mean they are a serious photographer.
exercises.explanation: No - they do a bit of photography but are not seriously into it. A dabbler never keeps doing one activity for long.

exercises.prompt: She's totally ___ football these days. She watches every match on TV.
exercises.explanation: Be hooked on something = be addicted to it.

exercises.prompt: What do you ___ when you aren't working, Nigel?
exercises.explanation: Get up to is the everyday informal way of asking what someone does in their free time.

exercises.prompt: *A:* I don't think I can fit in a tennis match with you for another couple of weeks. *B:* No problem. I've got a very ___ too.
exercises.explanation: A full diary (like a hectic social life) means you have a lot of activities booked.

exercises.answer: I went off football and I took up golf instead.
exercises.explanation: Go off something = lose interest in it; take up something = start it as a new hobby.
